proposals.name: Named referent is load-bearing (name-swap test)
proposals.instruction: Ask whether the joke survives substituting a different famous person, team, brand, or place for the one named. Score 10 when the entry collapses entirely under substitution because the humor depends on a specific, verifiable fact about that referent (their scandal, failure, reputation, or signature behavior). Score 5 when the name adds flavor but a handful of other names would work about as well. Score 0 when the name is interchangeable filler, or when no specific referent is invoked at all and the entry would read identically with any proper noun dropped in. Judge only the text; do not consider whether you personally find it funny.
proposals.rationale: R38 (Bobbitt / 'circumspectly') and R51 (Buttafuoco / 'penetratingly') are dead without those exact names, and both are dense_high_card_low; R44 (Hazelwood mooring a ship) is the same shape. By contrast R26 ('Detroit Embarrassed by Pacers') and R24 ('Land Mine Retriever') are card_high_dense_low and would read the same with any team or any dog breed. A scorecard that checks 'references a famous person or institution' as a box credits both classes equally.

proposals.name: Modifier does double duty and indicts the speaker
proposals.instruction: For entries built on an attributive tag (an adverb, an adjective, a verb of speaking), score how many independent jobs that one word performs. Score 10 when the modifier is simultaneously (a) a literal manner-of-speaking word, (b) a pun on a second sense, and (c) an accusation aimed at the specific speaker quoted. Score 5 when it puns but the pun has no bearing on who is speaking. Score 0 when the modifier is merely decorative, arbitrary, or absent. A high score requires all three jobs at once, not just a pun.
proposals.rationale: R33 ('cordially' = cordial/liquor, aimed at Ted Kennedy denying a drinking problem), R49 ('chafed rashly'), R13 ('aimlessly' for a pitcher who could not find the plate) and R07 ('asserted plainly' at Janet Reno) all sit at dense_pct .84-.94 with card_pct .25-.41. A bank that scores 'contains a pun' or 'contains an adverb' cannot separate a triple-duty modifier from a single-duty one, which is exactly the width of this gap.

proposals.name: Delivers the literal output form the prompt demands
proposals.instruction: Compare the entry against the exact artifact the prompt requests. Score 10 when the entry is that artifact and nothing else: a Jeopardy prompt yields a question, a 'things that will never happen' prompt yields the thing, a pidgin prompt yields the mistranslated text, a continuation prompt yields the continuation. Score 5 when the artifact is present but padded with framing the prompt did not ask for. Score 0 when the entry supplies only a heading, a category label, a lead-in, a source attribution, or an answer where a question was required, so that the requested artifact is simply absent from the text.
proposals.rationale: R21 ('Answer: Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim') and R31 ('Answer: A Squeegee and a Codpiece...') supply the stimulus instead of the required question; R16 and R41 supply only the category heading; R11 supplies only the 'In a letter I received from Russia' lead-in; R46 supplies only 'A Political Slogan That Will Never Make It:'. Every one of these is card_high (.73-.94) and dense_low (.14-.31). These read as clean, grammatical, well-formed text, which a criterion bank rewards, while containing no entry at all.

proposals.name: Leaves an inferential gap the reader must close
proposals.instruction: Score the amount of work the entry hands to the reader without abandoning them. Score 10 when the entry withholds the connective step, so the reader must supply a referent, a second meaning, or an implied scene, and the step is short enough to be taken instantly. Score 5 when the connection is stated but some flavor is implied. Score 0 when the entry explains its own mechanism, announces its own cleverness, spells out why it is funny, or has no gap because the observation is fully literal on its face.
proposals.rationale: R05 ('Chuck 3:16'), R03 ('Abandon Your Containers') and R48 ('I'M WITH STUPID') are dense .84-.95 against card .12-.26 and consist entirely of an unclosed gap. The opposite pole is card_high_dense_low: R52 announces its own anagram and calls it a playful gibe, R39 ends with 'I think you are missing the point here', and R42 narrates its own setup at length. A bank rewarding clarity, completeness, or explicit setup-payoff structure will invert this axis.

proposals.name: Payload lands on the final word or phrase
proposals.instruction: Locate the single element that carries the humor and score its position. Score 10 when it is the last word or last phrase, so that nothing follows the turn and the entry stops the instant it pays off. Score 5 when the payload sits mid-text with a short tail after it. Score 0 when the payload appears early and the entry continues past it, or when the text trails off into attribution, qualification, or restatement after the turn has already happened.
proposals.rationale: R23 ends on 'ma'am-eating shark', R30 on 'too yellow by far for champagne', R29 on 'bottomless', R38 on 'circumspectly' - all dense_pct .85-.99 with card_pct .26-.50. Card_high_dense_low items such as R43 and R39 front-load or bury the turn and then keep talking. Placement is invisible to per-property scoring that asks only whether a pun, rhyme, or twist exists somewhere in the text.

proposals.name: Economy: effect per word, with no self-commentary
proposals.instruction: Score the ratio of comic effect to word count. Score 10 for an entry of a few words that delivers a complete idea with no throat-clearing, no framing sentence, and no commentary on its own joke. Score 5 for an entry whose length is proportionate but that includes some avoidable setup. Score 0 for an entry that takes several sentences to reach a point a phrase could have made, or that appends explanation, apology, or meta-commentary. Judge economy relative to the idea being delivered, not against a fixed word count.
proposals.rationale: R53 ('Monosyllabic'), R01 ('True North'), R48 and R58 ('U.N. Resolution') are one to three words each and run dense .79-.86 against card .12-.32; the scorecard appears to read brevity as thinness. Conversely R42 and R52, both card_high_dense_low, are multi-sentence entries whose extra prose is elaboration a bank would credit as development or craft.

proposals.name: Entry enacts its own point rather than asserting it
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry performs the property it is about. Score 10 when the text is itself an instance of the thing it names, so that reading it demonstrates the claim (a word about brevity that is long, a garment that humiliates its own wearer, a slogan that does to the reader what it describes). Score 5 when the entry describes the property vividly but does not embody it. Score 0 when the entry only asserts or labels a property from the outside.
proposals.rationale: R53 ('Monosyllabic') is a five-syllable word denying its own syllable count; R48 ('I'M WITH STUPID') makes the wearer the referent; R03 ('Abandon Your Containers') turns the reader into the thing abandoned. All three are dense .84-.95, card .12-.26. Enactment is a relational property of the whole text and is systematically invisible to per-attribute scoring.

proposals.name: Contradiction is grounded in world fact, not dictionary antonymy
proposals.instruction: For entries turning on an internal contradiction, score where the contradiction comes from. Score 10 when the two halves are compatible in the dictionary and are made incompatible only by a known fact about the world (an institution that never resolves, a person who cannot remember, a chase that was not fast). Score 5 when the contradiction is half lexical and half factual. Score 0 when the two halves are simple antonyms, or when the pairing is merely odd rather than contradictory, so that no real-world claim is being made.
proposals.rationale: R58 ('U.N. Resolution'), R36 ('Reagan Memoirs'), R59 ('Low-Speed Chase') and R01 ('True North') are all dense .79-.91 against card .27-.42; each asserts a factual indictment through an apparently innocuous noun phrase. Card_high_dense_low items like R20 ('Precision Pi Calculator') and R10 ('Lesser Hyattsville') are lexically odd but make no claim about anything. A bank scoring 'contains a contradiction' cannot see the difference.

proposals.name: Parses as sense, then self-cancels in exactly one step
proposals.instruction: Score the two-stage structure of pseudo-wisdom. Score 10 when the sentence reads on first pass as ordinary practical advice or observation, and collapses into vacuity or self-contradiction after precisely one step of reasoning that the reader takes unaided. Score 5 when the collapse takes several steps, or when the sentence is visibly odd on first reading so there is no first-pass plausibility to lose. Score 0 when the sentence is either straightforwardly true, or nonsense from the opening words with no surface of sense at all.
proposals.rationale: R15 (VCRs let you see shows without watching them), R54 (confusion about Central America as the mark of understanding), R57 (the lottery odds if you have all six numbers) and R35 (religion requires belief) run dense .80-.93 against card .21-.44. The bank presumably credits 'is paradoxical' or 'is self-contradictory', which fires equally on flat nonsense; the timing of the collapse is what separates these.

proposals.name: Ventriloquism: the quoted line matches the speaker's real idiom
proposals.instruction: When the entry puts words in a named person's mouth, score how convincingly the diction, grammar, and register match that person's known speech. Score 10 when the sentence could be lifted verbatim from the person, including their characteristic errors, evasions, or verbal tics. Score 5 when the content fits the person but the voice is neutral or generic. Score 0 when the diction actively contradicts the speaker, or when the quoted line is written in a bland authorial register indistinguishable from any other entry.
proposals.rationale: R51 ('I never done nothing to that girl') reproduces its speaker's grammar, and R57 ('that ain't so if you got all six numbers') reproduces its speaker's cadence; both are dense_high_card_low at .96 and .92 dense. R33 does the same with a stiff denial. A scorecard checking 'quotes a famous person' or 'is in dialogue form' scores voice-matched and voice-neutral quotations identically.

proposals.name: Meter holds, and the strained rhyme is itself the joke
proposals.instruction: For verse entries, score meter and rhyme jointly. Score 10 when the lines scan cleanly in the form's expected rhythm AND any distorted, invented, or contorted rhyme word reads as a deliberate comic move rather than a failure. Score 5 when the meter holds but the rhymes are merely competent, or when a strained rhyme is present but reads as unintentional. Score 0 when lines do not scan, when line lengths wander without effect, or when the rhyme scheme breaks down. Judge the form as executed on the page.
proposals.rationale: R14 (dense .98 / card .39) invents 'forlorner' to match 'Tysons Corner' and the strain is the payoff; R23 (dense .99 / card .48) and R30 (dense .99 / card .50) scan cleanly and turn on the final rhyme; R29 (dense .80 / card .25) builds a rhymed escalation. These four are the top of the dense side, which suggests the bank scores rhyme presence and meter separately and misses that a bad rhyme can be good.

proposals.name: Sound-tweak carries an added claim beyond the tweak
proposals.instruction: For entries built by altering a familiar name, brand, or title, score what the alteration buys. Score 10 when the altered form both sounds like the original AND asserts something pointed and true about its referent, so that a reader learns a judgment from the substitution. Score 5 when the alteration produces a coherent second meaning that is merely incongruous. Score 0 when the alteration is purely phonetic - one letter or syllable changed for the sound of it - and the resulting phrase makes no claim, or when the alteration produces a phrase that means nothing at all.
proposals.rationale: R12 ('Golden Reliever'), R09 ('WordPrefect'), R60 ('Peace Corpse'), R50 ('Profiles in Scourge') and R24 ('Land Mine Retriever') are all card_high (.69-.94) and dense_low (.13-.28): mechanically clean, semantically empty substitutions. R59 ('Low-Speed Chase') and R05 ('Chuck 3:16') are the same mechanism carrying an actual claim, and sit at dense .82-.84 with card .12-.27. This is the single largest visible cluster in the card_high_dense_low half.

proposals.name: Referent is recognizable without homework
proposals.instruction: Score how much prior knowledge the entry demands before any humor is available. Score 10 when the referent is a person, event, product, or phrase a general newspaper reader recognizes immediately and the joke fires on first reading. Score 5 when the referent is somewhat specialized but the entry supplies enough context to carry a reader who does not know it. Score 0 when the entry cannot be understood at all without specialist or trivia knowledge and supplies no scaffolding. Score the demand made on a general reader, not the obscurity of the topic in the abstract.
proposals.rationale: R21 (Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim), R22 (Gheorge Muresan) and R19 (Marilyn Vos Savant's puzzle) are card .76-.94 against dense .11-.17: each is well formed and internally correct but inert without trivia. The dense-favored referents (R38 Bobbitt, R44 Hazelwood, R48) were unmissable. Correctness-shaped criteria score a well-executed obscure reference as high as a well-executed familiar one.

proposals.name: Transgression is carried by construction, not supplied raw
proposals.instruction: When an entry reaches for offensive, cruel, or taboo material, score how much comic construction sits between the reader and the raw material. Score 10 when the transgressive element is delivered through a mechanism - a pun, a reversal, an understatement, a formal constraint - so that the construction, not the shock, is what produces the effect. Score 5 when there is some framing but the shock does most of the work. Score 0 when the entry consists of a slur, an atrocity, or a taboo image presented with no transformation, so that naming the thing is the entire content.
proposals.rationale: R34 ('Hymietown') and R06 ('Sim Cambodian Death Camp') are card .93 and .96 against dense .37 and .28: both are formally responsive to their prompts and both are unconstructed shock. R38 handles a mutilation through a single-word pun and R29 handles indecency through rhymed escalation, and both are dense_high_card_low. A bank with an edginess, boldness, or willingness-to-offend criterion will reward the raw versions most.

proposals.name: Engages the prompt's specific conceit, not just its category
proposals.instruction: Read the qualifying language in the prompt - the adjective, the twist, the stated purpose - and score whether the entry answers that qualifier or only the broad category. Score 10 when the entry could only have been written for this exact prompt because it turns on the qualifier itself. Score 5 when the entry fits the category well and glances at the qualifier. Score 0 when the entry satisfies the category generically and would serve equally well as a submission to a differently-qualified version of the same prompt.
proposals.rationale: The T-shirt prompt asks for the transcendent indignity of this contest, and R48, R03 and R05 all target self-humiliation specifically (dense .84-.95, card .12-.26). R55 ('It Had to Be You' for Adam and Eve) turns exactly on the 'should not play' qualifier at dense .85 / card .21. Meanwhile R10 ('Lesser Hyattsville') and R47 ('Palookaville, USA') are card .78-.98 against dense .25-.28 and are generic bad names not fitted to any particular category. A bank scoring 'responds to the prompt' at category granularity credits both.

proposals.name: Raw verbosity: total word count of the entry
proposals.instruction: Count the words of the entry text, excluding any trailing parenthetical name-and-city block, and convert to a 0-10 extent score: 0 for 1-3 words, 2 for 4-7, 4 for 8-14, 6 for 15-24, 8 for 25-40, 10 for more than 40. Report the extent only. You must NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the entry is too long or too short, or whether brevity suits the prompt. This is a measurement, not an evaluation.
proposals.rationale: The slice is strongly bimodal in length and the two models split on it. Three-word entries such as R54 ('I'M WITH STUPID', dense .954 / card .261), R49 ('Monosyllabic', .827 / .224) and R14 ('Chuck 3:16', .843 / .117) sit at the extreme dense-high end while the scorecard buries them; multi-sentence entries such as R41 (35 words, dense .333 / card .866) and R20 (dense .393 / card .949) sit at the opposite corner. Word count is a pure counting feature that any text model can latch onto, and it is not itself how good an entry is - a one-word oxymoron and a five-line limerick can both be excellent.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Trailing parenthetical attribution block present and long
proposals.instruction: Score how much trailing attribution apparatus appears at the end of the entry: a parenthetical containing personal names and place names. Score 0 when there is none, 3 when a single name-and-city appears, 6 when a name-and-city plus a second locality or an out-of-state marker appears, and 10 when the parenthetical runs to multiple full names with cities. Score only the presence and size of this block. You must NOT judge whether attribution is desirable, nor let the block's contents influence your reading of the joke itself.
proposals.rationale: Attribution blocks are present in roughly half the slice and absent in the other half in a way that tracks nothing about the writing: R04 carries three full name-and-city pairs (card .944), R59 and R47 carry one each, while R54, R11, R43 and R45 carry none. The block is editorial furniture added downstream of the entrant, not part of the entry, and its presence adds tokens, proper nouns and punctuation that a text-only model can read as signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: corpus construction and archival formatting - whether the byline survived transcription into the dataset

proposals.name: Convergent attribution: multiple independent entrants credited
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the attribution indicates that more than one person submitted this same item independently. Score 0 when a single entrant or none is named, 5 when two names appear or the word 'also' introduces a second submitter, and 10 when three or more separate name-and-city entries are listed. Score the visible multiplicity of credited submitters only. You must NOT infer or judge anything about the entry's merit from how many people are credited.
proposals.rationale: R04 lists three submitters (card .944 / dense .405), R35 uses the explicit 'also' construction, and R44 and R30 each list two. Convergence is a fingerprint of an idea's availability, which is a property of the prompt-plus-population rather than of the writing. Tagged mixed because a phrase several sharp entrants independently found may also be genuinely apt, so the parent plausibly causes real quality as well as this fingerprint.
proposals.upstream_parent: independent co-discovery - how many entrants arrived at the same idea, i.e. how obvious the idea was given the prompt

proposals.name: Truncation residue: fragment, dangling colon, mid-sentence stop
proposals.instruction: Score how much the text reads as a cut-off or partial capture rather than a complete submission. Score 10 when it stops mid-sentence or mid-phrase, ends on a bare colon or dash, or consists solely of a heading, a title, a category label, a lead-in, or a quoted stimulus with no response attached. Score 5 when it is grammatically complete but conspicuously missing a component the prompt names. Score 0 when the text is a whole, self-contained submission. Score the extent of the truncation fingerprint only. You must NOT judge whether the fragment is nonetheless witty.
proposals.rationale: R38 stops mid-sentence at 'This is a beguiling' and is the single highest dense item in the slice at dense .999; R21 ('Something That Will Never Become') stops mid-phrase; R32 ends on a bare '--'; R37 and R29 end on bare colons; R52 is a title alone; R36 and R40 are quoted stimuli with no continuation. These fragments land at both extremes of the disagreement, which is the signature of a scraping artifact rather than of writing quality: nothing about the entrant produced the cut.
proposals.upstream_parent: corpus extraction and segmentation - how the archived contest column was split into per-entry records

proposals.name: Washington-area place-name density in text or byline
proposals.instruction: Score how saturated the item is with Washington-metro geography. Count distinct local toponyms (Tysons Corner, Takoma Park, McLean, Hyattsville, Bethesda, Arlington, Fairfax, Columbia, Vienna, Falls Church, Silver Spring, and similar) appearing anywhere in the entry or its attribution. Score 0 for none, 4 for one, 7 for two, 10 for three or more, and reduce by 3 if the only place names present are outside the Washington region. Score density only. You must NOT judge whether the local reference is well used or whether locality is appropriate to the prompt.
proposals.rationale: R05, R09 and R18 each name a local town in the first line and sit at dense .981-.987; R42 ('Lesser Hyattsville') is card .778 / dense .249; out-of-area bylines cluster on the other side, R10 (Savannah, card .983), R47 (Beaumont, Tex., card .962) and R08 (San Diego). Locality is a marker of which container an item came from and of the entrant's address, not of craft. Tagged mixed because one contest in this slice explicitly requires a Washington-area place, so local geography is partly a real prompt-compliance signal there.
proposals.upstream_parent: venue and audience - a local newspaper contest whose entrants and readers are concentrated in one metro area

proposals.name: Conformity to a rigid shared syntactic or prosodic template
proposals.instruction: Score how closely the entry matches a fixed structural mold shared with other entries of its type: paired quotation marks followed by a named speaker and a single adverb; five short lines in an AABBA rhyme layout; a two-turn call-and-response; a headline with no verb inflection. Score 10 when the entry reproduces such a mold slot-for-slot with no deviation, 5 when it follows a loose recognisable shape, 0 when it has no template structure. Score structural conformity only. You must NOT judge whether the template is executed well or whether following it is a merit.
proposals.rationale: Eight items in the slice reproduce the quote-plus-name-plus-adverb mold exactly (R06, R07, R19, R22, R25, R26, R27, R58) and every one of them is dense_high_card_low; three more reproduce the five-line verse layout (R05, R09, R18) at dense .981-.987. Template conformity is largely container identity leaking into the text - it says which week's contest this is, which a text-only model can exploit. Tagged mixed because executing a hard form cleanly is also partly genuine craft.
proposals.upstream_parent: which contest container the item came from, together with the entrant's prior practice at that recurring format

proposals.name: Density of early-1990s news-cycle proper nouns
proposals.instruction: Score how many references to people, institutions or events that were prominent in the news of a narrow period appear in the entry. Count named public figures, current officeholders, athletes, litigants, scandals and product names. Score 0 for none, 4 for one, 7 for two, 10 for three or more; add nothing for how apt the reference is. Score topical-name density only. You must NOT judge whether the reference is funny, well chosen, or recognisable to you.
proposals.rationale: R07 (Bobbitt), R25 (Buttafuoco), R27 (Hazelwood) and R58 (Ted Kennedy) are dense .851-.960 and card .272-.428; R59 (Gheorge Muresan) and R47 (Marilyn Vos Savant) carry the same kind of marker at the opposite corner, card .837 and .962 against dense .128 and .399. The density of period-specific names is set by when the contest ran, not by the entrant's skill, and it gives a text model a strong date and container cue.
proposals.upstream_parent: the publication date of the contest and the news cycle running that week

proposals.name: Taboo, bodily or atrocity lexical content
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the entry's lexical content is drawn from taboo registers: sexual or anatomical terms, excretory or exposure terms, ethnic slurs, mass violence, death and corpses. Score 0 when none is present, 4 when a single mild term appears, 7 when a taboo term is the entry's central noun phrase, and 10 when the entry consists substantially of such material. Score lexical presence and prominence only. You must NOT judge whether the material is handled well, whether it is gratuitous, or whether it offends you.
proposals.rationale: Taboo lexis appears at both extremes of the disagreement, which is exactly what a nuisance channel looks like: R30 ('Hymietown', card .926 / dense .370) and R53 ('Sim Cambodian Death Camp', card .959 / dense .276) on one side, R01 ('I'd moon the Super Bowl', dense .804 / card .248) and R26 (underwear, dense .862 / card .370) on the other, with R43 ('Codpiece') and R47 ('breasts') also in the mix. A keyword-sensitive scorer can key on the register itself, which is a topic fact and not a quality fact.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Found-object provenance framing before the payload
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the entry opens with a claim about where its text came from rather than simply presenting the text: phrases naming a sign, a letter, a menu, a translation, a source document, a quoted number or a location of discovery. Score 10 when a full provenance clause precedes the payload, 5 when a short source tag or numbered quote label precedes it, 0 when the entry begins directly with its own content. Score the presence and length of the framing only. You must NOT judge whether the framing adds charm or whether the provenance claim is credible.
proposals.rationale: R24 opens with 'From a sign in the garden of a Thai temple at Chang Mai' (dense .982 / card .486) while R29 is nothing but the provenance clause 'In a letter I received from Russia after visiting my pen pals:' (dense .306 / card .894); R36 and R40 carry the numbered 'Quote 1:' / 'Quote 7:' source labels. The framing is an artifact of how the material was obtained and how the column was laid out, not a property of the joke. Tagged mixed because genuinely found absurdity may also be funnier than invented absurdity.
proposals.upstream_parent: mode of production - transcribing real found text encountered in the world versus composing the item outright, and the extra travel or correspondence context that implies

proposals.name: First-obvious-reading of the prompt versus late-arriving riff
proposals.instruction: MODE 3 - position fingerprint. Score how much the entry reads like the first thing a competent person would produce on reading the prompt, as opposed to something written by someone who has already exhausted the obvious takes. Score 0 for the most available response: a single stock phrase with one letter or syllable altered, a dictionary-level pairing, the canonical example of the category. Score 5 for a response requiring one non-obvious pivot. Score 10 for a response that argues with the prompt, answers a different question than the one asked, addresses the contest itself, or presupposes that the obvious takes are already used up. Score availability-of-the-idea only. You must NOT judge whether obvious or late responses are better; both ends can be excellent or terrible.
proposals.rationale: The most-available responses cluster hard in card_high_dense_low: R11 ('Peace Corpse'), R23 ('Profiles in Scourge'), R50 ('Golden Reliever'), R28 ('Land Mine Retriever') and R16 (the cancan) are each the first phonetic tweak the prompt invites, at card .691-.938 against dense .109-.284. The far end - R33, which refuses the comparison task and answers on a spelling technicality (card .977), and R41, which turns the excuse prompt onto the contest itself (card .866) - reads as written by someone who had already seen the obvious takes taken. Position and timing in the entry stream are not properties of how good an entry is, but they leave this availability fingerprint in the text. Tagged mixed because entrants writing deep into their own attempt list may also be more practised writers.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream and submission timing - where in the week's flood of submissions, and how deep into an entrant's own list of attempts, an item was produced

proposals.name: Adverb ironically maps onto named figure's real reputation
proposals.instruction: Score how sharply the entry's adverb (or other descriptive tag on a quoted line) creates a SECOND, ironic meaning once read against the named person's well-known real-world reputation or situation, beyond simply describing the tone of delivery. A 10: the adverb is bland/generic taken alone but becomes pointedly apt once connected to a specific, widely-known fact about the person, recontextualizing the whole line. A 0: the adverb is purely a manner-of-speaking descriptor with no connection to any real-world fact about the person, or there is no named-person/quote structure at all.
proposals.rationale: R11 ("circumspectly" ironically undercutting John Bobbitt) and R43 ("cantankerously" tied to Capt. Hazelwood's real notoriety) are dense_high_card_low; this ironic real-world-fact mapping is exactly the kind of extratextual, layered irony a fixed criterion bank might miss while a broadly-informed reader perceives it directly.

proposals.name: Aphoristic wisdom-voice that logically collapses on inspection
proposals.instruction: Score how well the entry mimics the voice of confident folk-wisdom ("the thing about X is...") while the underlying logic is actually circular, tautological, or a non sequitur that falls apart on a second read. 10 = entry sounds like genuine sage advice on first read and only on reflection reveals it says nothing or contradicts itself. 0 = entry is a plain true or plain false statement, or does not attempt the wisdom-voice framing at all.
proposals.rationale: R01 ("Anyone who isn't confused about Central America doesn't understand it") and R55 ("They say the lottery is an 80 million-to-one shot, but that ain't so if you got all six numbers") are dense_high_card_low examples of this exact paradox-collapse structure, which depends on recognizing a rhetorical form rather than any single scorable fact.

proposals.name: Full multi-line structural completion, not a fragment
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which the entry executes a COMPLETE multi-part form (e.g. all five limerick lines with consistent meter and AABBA rhyme, or a full narrative arc) rather than delivering only a title, a fragment, or a single clever line. 10 = every structural unit the invoked form requires is present and internally consistent. 0 = entry is a title only, a sentence fragment, or otherwise stops well short of the form it invokes.
proposals.rationale: R20 and R23 are complete, technically executed limericks (dense_high_card_low), while R04 ("The Secret Agent's Lament") is only a title with no poem body yet is also dense_high_card_low -- separating the two lets us test whether full-form execution specifically is under-credited by the scorecard bank.

proposals.name: Punchline held to the final words, reframing what came before
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry's surprise or payoff is concentrated in the FINAL few words, such that a reader must re-interpret everything before it once they arrive there. 10 = the last word or short phrase recontextualizes the entire preceding text and is unpredictable from what came before. 0 = the payoff, if any, is evident from the opening words and the ending adds nothing new.
proposals.rationale: R20 ("...encountered a ma'am-eating shark") and R55 ("...if you got all six numbers") both withhold their real payoff to the last words and are dense_high_card_low, suggesting delayed-reveal timing is rewarded by the dense model more than by a static criterion bank.

proposals.name: Sustained, distinct persona voice throughout the entry
proposals.instruction: Score how consistently the entry maintains ONE distinct, recognizable voice or register (e.g. folksy sage, gruff sea captain, terse slogan) from start to finish, versus drifting between registers or reading as generic. 10 = every word choice reinforces a single identifiable persona. 0 = the entry has no discernible persona, or mixes incompatible registers within a few words.
proposals.rationale: R09 (sustained Yogi Berra folk-wisdom voice) and R43 (sustained gruff-captain voice via "cantankerously" plus the in-character dialogue) are both dense_high_card_low; voice consistency is a property spanning multiple prompt categories that a per-category criterion bank might not capture uniformly.

proposals.name: Elaboration added beyond a bare single-word substitution pun
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry ADDS (a scene, a second meaning, an attributed voice, extra context) beyond the mechanical trick of swapping one word or morpheme in a familiar phrase or brand name. 10 = the swap is embedded in enough surrounding context to produce a second, independent laugh or insight beyond the swap itself. 0 = the entry IS the swapped phrase and nothing else; the joke is fully exhausted the instant the swap is recognized.
proposals.rationale: R08 ("Peace Corpse") and R52 ("Golden Reliever") are one-word-swap bad-names with zero elaboration, both card_high_dense_low; this suggests the scorecard bank may reward the mere presence of a recognizable substitution mechanism regardless of whether anything is built on top of it.

proposals.name: Real-world reference adds irony, not just recognition
proposals.instruction: Score whether recognizing a specific real person, place, or event adds a genuine irony, twist, or critique on top of the bare fact, versus the entry merely repeating an already-odd-sounding true fact with no additional wit layered on. 10 = the reference is deployed to create a punchline that would not exist without an authorial twist. 0 = the entry states a factual curiosity with no added twist -- the "joke" is just "isn't this fact odd".
proposals.rationale: R43 (Hazelwood's real Exxon Valdez notoriety ironically colliding with "cantankerously... mooring this ship") is dense_high_card_low and shows an added twist, whereas R14 ("Answer: Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim") is card_high_dense_low and appears to rest on the bare oddity of a real historical name with no further twist supplied.

proposals.name: Entry text is complete, not cut off mid-thought
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry reads as a self-contained, finished unit of text versus appearing to break off before a clause, sentence, or thought is finished. 10 = entry is unambiguously complete as given. 0 = entry visibly stops mid-sentence or mid-clause with no closing punctuation resolving the thought.
proposals.rationale: R28 ("(Cartoon A) This is a beguiling") is dense_high_card_low and reads as cut off mid-sentence, while R24 ("Something That Will Never Become") is card_high_dense_low and is similarly truncated; textual completeness shows up on both sides of the disagreement and deserves direct scoring rather than an assumption that truncation always signals corpus noise.

proposals.name: Conceptual distance between yoked terms that still coheres
proposals.instruction: For entries that juxtapose two concepts (oxymorons, mash-up names), score how far apart the two joined concepts are while still resolving into a single coherent, apt image. 10 = the two concepts are maximally distant or contradictory yet click together sensibly and aptly. 0 = the two concepts are near-synonyms, or so distant that no coherent single image results.
proposals.rationale: R30 ("Low-Speed Chase") and R22 ("U.N. Resolution") both yoke a dramatic/decisive concept to its anticlimactic opposite and are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards well-resolved conceptual distance more than the scorecard does.

proposals.name: Entry's own form embodies or enacts its content
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry's linguistic form demonstrates or contradicts the very property it names or describes (self-reference), rather than merely describing that property from outside. 10 = the form is inseparable from the content -- the entry could not make its point without exhibiting the property itself. 0 = form and content are unrelated; the entry simply states something without enacting it.
proposals.rationale: R51 ("Monosyllabic" as an oxymoron because the word itself has five syllables) is a clean self-demonstrating joke and is dense_high_card_low; R35 ("The High School SAT Preperation Kit", where "Preperation" is itself misspelled) similarly enacts its own point and is card_high_dense_low -- self-demonstration cuts across the disagreement in both directions.

proposals.name: In-text irregularity reads as clearly intentional, not noise
proposals.instruction: Score how unambiguously a spelling or grammar irregularity in the entry is signaled as INTENTIONAL and load-bearing for the joke, as opposed to being indistinguishable from an accidental typo or a transcription/formatting artifact. 10 = impossible to read the irregularity as anything but a deliberate joke given the surrounding context. 0 = the irregularity could easily be mistaken for noise, with nothing signaling it is meant as humor.
proposals.rationale: R35's "Preperation" typo is legible as intentional once the SAT-prep irony is noticed (card_high_dense_low); by contrast R28's abrupt cutoff ("...This is a beguiling") is much harder to read confidently as a deliberate device rather than a corpus artifact (dense_high_card_low) -- distinguishing signaled-intentional wordplay from ambiguous noise is a judgment a rigid criterion bank might not make reliably.

proposals.name: Multiple independent submitters credited for the same entry
proposals.instruction: Score, inversely, how many separately named submitters or locations are credited for essentially the same wording, as a proxy for how independently "findable" the underlying idea was. 10 = a single or no attributed submitter, or an attribution specific enough to suggest an idiosyncratic idea. 0 = two or more independently credited submitters arrived at the same or near-identical wording.
proposals.rationale: R13 ("True North", credited to David Kuebrich AND, separately, Chuck Nelson) and R47 ("Reagan Memoirs", credited to Jessica Steinhice AND, separately, L. Woodall) both show multiple independent convergence yet are dense_high_card_low, a useful test of whether either model is sensitive to idea-obviousness signaled directly in the credit line.

proposals.name: Self-contained logical or lexical riddle operation
proposals.instruction: Score how cleanly the entry works as a self-contained riddle -- a precise logical inversion, category trick, or lexical operation performed on the prompt's own constraint -- that resolves without requiring any outside cultural knowledge. 10 = an elegant, symmetric logical or lexical twist a reader can verify using only the prompt and the entry text. 0 = no logical or lexical operation is present; the entry is a flat statement or requires outside facts to make sense.
proposals.rationale: R17 ("What is the opposite of a head count?") is a clean self-contained inversion of the prompt's own premise, and R12 (identifying the item that "does not belong" because the other two share the letter "M") substitutes a lexical trick for the expected semantic category; both are card_high_dense_low, suggesting the scorecard rewards this closed-form riddle logic more than the dense model does.

proposals.name: Entry breaks frame to comment on itself or the contest
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry steps outside its ostensible task to comment on its own quality, on the contest, or on the act of judging or submitting, with that self-aware commentary itself constituting the joke. 10 = the entry is substantially or entirely meta-commentary that succeeds as humor about the contest or joke-making process itself. 0 = the entry stays entirely within the fiction of the prompt with no acknowledgment of the contest or of itself as an entry.
proposals.rationale: R25 (explaining, in-character as a New Yorker cartoon editor, that an unfunny cartoon's caption is secretly an anagram for "Little Weak") and R36 (a full first-person essay about the experience of entering the Style Invitational itself) both use frame-breaking self-awareness as their core device and are card_high_dense_low.

proposals.name: Flat institutional or clinical register applied to absurd content
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry adopts a flat, official, clinical, or reference-book register (e.g. dictionary definition, trivia-answer phrasing, book-title convention) to present content that is actually absurd or dark, generating comedy from the mismatch between register and content. 10 = the entry is indistinguishable in tone from genuine official or reference prose while the substance is absurd. 0 = the entry's register is expressive, informal, or exclamatory throughout, with no institutional-deadpan contrast.
proposals.rationale: R08 ("Who founded the Peace Corpse?", phrased with flat trivia-question neutrality despite the dark pun) and R53 ("Who wrote \"Profiles in Scourge\"?", mimicking a straight bibliographic question) both rely on this deadpan-register-vs-dark-content mismatch and are card_high_dense_low.

proposals.name: Raw word/token length of the entry text
proposals.instruction: Count or estimate the total number of words in the ENTRY text only, excluding the attribution parenthetical. Score 0 = extremely short (a title, a single phrase, under about 5 words) up to 10 = long, multi-sentence text (a full poem, paragraph, or multi-clause joke). This is a pure length measurement -- do not judge whether the length is appropriate or whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: R44 and R54 are full four/five-line limericks (dense_high_card_low) while R02 and R25 are single short sentences (dense_low_card_high); if raw length tracks the split independent of any judged wit, it is a nuisance the discounted readout should strip out.
proposals.upstream_parent: entry format/category (some prompts structurally demand short outputs, others long ones) and possible editorial space constraints on how much text a given slot in the print column can hold

proposals.name: Presence of parenthetical name-plus-city attribution
proposals.instruction: Score how much of a standard "(Name, City)" or "(Name, City; also, Name, City)" attribution parenthetical appears at the end of the entry. 0 = no attribution present at all. 10 = a full, standard attribution with name and city (or multiple names). Score only whether/how much this formatting element is present -- do not judge whether the entry itself is good.
proposals.rationale: R06 ("I'M WITH STUPID") and R09 ("The Secret Agent's Lament") carry no attribution and are dense_high_card_low, while R25 and R46 carry full "(Name, City)" attributions and are dense_low_card_high; attribution presence may simply track which processing stage/list an item was pulled from, not its quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: which stage or column of the newspaper's publication process an entry came from (e.g. a final printed winners list with credits vs an unattributed draft/finalist pool)

proposals.name: Use of full capitalization or exclamatory punctuation
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the entry text uses ALL-CAPS words or exclamation points as an emphasis device, independent of content. 0 = entry uses standard sentence case throughout with no exclamation marks. 10 = entry is entirely or mostly capitalized, or uses multiple exclamation points. Score the typographic extent only, not whether the emphasis is effective or funny.
proposals.rationale: R06 ("I'M WITH STUPID") is fully capitalized and dense_high_card_low, while R19 and R38, from the very same T-shirt-slogan prompt, use standard title/sentence case and are also dense_high_card_low -- capitalization varies within a single prompt/category regardless of the dense/card split, making it a plausible typographic nuisance rather than a quality signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Entry text ends abruptly without closing punctuation or sense
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry appears to break off before completing a sentence or clause -- e.g. ending on a dash, a colon, a dangling preposition, or simply stopping without terminal punctuation that resolves the thought. 0 = entry is clearly a complete, self-contained unit. 10 = entry unmistakably stops mid-clause or mid-sentence. Score only the extent of apparent incompleteness in the text as given -- do not judge whether an incomplete-looking entry is still funny or good.
proposals.rationale: R14 ("...Olympic Sport --") and R23 ("Something That Will Never Become") both look cut off and are dense_low_card_high, while R47 ("(Cartoon A) This is a beguiling") also looks cut off and is dense_high_card_low -- apparent truncation shows up on both sides of the disagreement, consistent with a corpus-extraction artifact rather than a quality signal either model is correctly tracking.
proposals.upstream_parent: how the item was extracted or paginated from the original print column into this corpus (a mining/parsing artifact), independent of anything the entrant wrote

proposals.name: Entry copies boilerplate scaffold text from the prompt sheet
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the entry consists of literal scaffold/header text apparently copied from the contest worksheet itself (e.g. the words "Answer:", "Quote N:", or similar labels) rather than being freely composed by the entrant. 0 = no such scaffold text present. 10 = the entry opens with or consists substantially of such a copied label. Score only the presence of this copied boilerplate, not whether the entry built on top of it is good.
proposals.rationale: R33 ("Answer: A Squeegee...") and R36 ("Answer: Theophrastus...") both carry the copied "Answer:" scaffold label and are dense_low_card_high, while R41 ("Quote 1: ...") and R56 ("Quote 7: ...") carry a parallel copied "Quote N:" scaffold label and are dense_high_card_low -- the same boilerplate-copying habit appears on both sides of the split, suggesting a worksheet/corpus artifact rather than a quality signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Density of dated, real-world scandal or news proper nouns
proposals.instruction: Score how many specific, datable real-world proper nouns (named public figures, named news events, named brands tied to a specific incident) appear in the entry, weighted toward ones recognizable only to someone following the news closely around the time of writing. 0 = no such proper nouns. 10 = entry is built entirely around several highly specific, dated real-world references. Score only the density/specificity of such references -- do not judge whether the references are used cleverly.
proposals.rationale: R07 (Bobbitt), R18 (Buttafuoco), R39 (Hazelwood/Exxon Valdez), R58 (Ted Kennedy), and R59 (Janet Reno) are all Tom Swiftly entries anchored to specific, dated tabloid/political scandals and are dense_high_card_low; if recognizing the reference, rather than any wit added to it, drives the dense score, that recognition-based boost is a nuisance, though it is plausibly entangled with real comic timing skill, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: temporal proximity between the entry's submission and a salient news cycle (a submission-timing/zeitgeist effect on the receiving audience's recognition and enjoyment), and possible reader/editor recency bias

proposals.name: Multiple independently credited submitters for one entry
proposals.instruction: Score how many separately named submitters (connected by "also," or similar) are credited for what is presented as essentially the same entry. 0 = a single submitter or no attribution at all. 10 = three or more independently credited submitters for the same wording. Score only the count/extent of multiple crediting, not whether the shared idea is good.
proposals.rationale: R03 ("Hymietown", two submitters), R04 ("WordPrefect", two submitters), and R12 (three submitters) are all dense_low_card_high, while R53 ("Reagan Memoirs") and R57 ("True North") each carry two credited submitters and are dense_high_card_low -- multi-submitter crediting appears on both sides, making it worth isolating as a possible nuisance about idea-obviousness or editorial crediting habits rather than actual quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: how obvious or independently-discoverable the underlying idea was to the broader entrant pool, and the editors' practice of crediting all independent duplicates rather than picking one

proposals.name: Entry's grammatical form literally matches the prompt's required response type
proposals.instruction: Score how strictly the entry's surface grammatical form matches the literal response type the prompt calls for (e.g. for a "what are the questions" prompt, whether the entry is literally phrased as an interrogative sentence ending in "?"; for a "propose a name" prompt, whether the entry is literally a short name/noun phrase rather than a sentence). 0 = entry's grammatical form does not match the literally requested type at all. 10 = entry's form is a textbook-exact match to the requested type. Score only the grammatical form match, not whether the content is witty.
proposals.rationale: R25 ("What is the opposite of a head count?") and R35 ("What are the ending steps in the cancan?") are textbook-exact interrogative matches to the Jeopardy prompt's required form and are dense_low_card_high; testing whether mere rule-conformity, rather than the joke inside it, drives the scorecard's score here would help isolate a process-driven nuisance from genuine wit.
proposals.upstream_parent: editorial/receiving-side filtering that may favor entries which are easy to typeset or verify as satisfying the rules, independent of how funny they are

proposals.name: Directness of entry as the most obvious reading of the prompt
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry reads as the single most direct, literal, first-instinct response to the prompt's wording, as opposed to a lateral, unexpected, or second-order angle on it. 0 = the entry approaches the prompt from a surprising or oblique angle unlikely to be anyone's first idea. 10 = the entry is close to the most obvious, straightforward way to satisfy the prompt's literal ask. Score only how obvious or direct the reading is -- do not judge whether an obvious or unobvious reading is better.
proposals.rationale: R08 ("the stupid rodent does not belong because the other two things begin with M") answers the "what does not belong and why" prompt via a fairly direct, literal category-logic move and is dense_low_card_high, while R05 ("U.N. Resolution") requires an oblique, non-obvious angle on "oxymoron for our times" and is dense_high_card_low; if obviousness-of-take tracks an early-arrival effect in the submission stream rather than the entry's own cleverness, it should be discounted as a position nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream -- whether the item was likely conceived early, before other obvious takes were used up, or arrived after many similar entries had already been submitted

proposals.name: Explicit self-reference to the contest or being a repeat entrant
proposals.instruction: Score how much the entry explicitly names or describes the contest itself (e.g. "Style Invitational"), a past round of it, or the entrant's own history of submitting to it, as opposed to staying entirely inside the fictional or topical world the prompt asks for. 0 = no mention of the contest or the act of entering it. 10 = the entry is substantially about the contest itself or the entrant's relationship to it. Score only the presence of this self-reference, not whether it is used cleverly.
proposals.rationale: R37 ("Entering the Style Invitational: I used to enter Publishers Clearing House sweepstakes...") explicitly frames itself around the contest and the entrant's own submitting history, and is dense_low_card_high; this in-group, community-facing move may be rewarded by explicit scorecard criteria while reflecting insider tenure more than intrinsic wit, though a genuinely funnier veteran voice is also plausible, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's tenure/insider status within the regular entrant community (in-group familiarity with the contest's own running jokes and conventions)

proposals.name: Self-Refuting Premise
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording cleanly invalidates itself and that self-cancellation is the joke; score 0 when no internal contradiction exists or it is accidental.
proposals.rationale: R52 makes the word’s syllable count contradict its meaning, while R45 and R60 turn literal exceptions into the punch. These show compact self-cancellation that weaker literal formulations lack.

proposals.name: Adverbial Semantic Snap
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a quoted statement and its manner adverb are both natural yet jointly expose a second meaning; score 0 when the adverb is merely decorative.
proposals.rationale: R09, R21, and R51 pair denials with adverbs that undercut or reframe them. R44 and R56 show the same mechanism, beyond simply mentioning a famous person.

proposals.name: Prompt-Form Fusion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the required form actively creates the joke’s timing, meaning, or payoff; score 0 when the same joke would work unchanged in any format.
proposals.rationale: R08, R47, and R53 use limerick structure to carry setup into punch. R55 suggests why rhyme alone is insufficient without form reinforcing the comic mechanism.

proposals.name: High Joke Density
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when nearly every word performs comic work and a complete premise is delivered economically; score 0 when brevity produces a generic, thin, or unfinished entry.
proposals.rationale: R06, R07, R14, and R42 achieve complete effects in very few words, whereas R15 and R23 use more language without a comparably focused mechanism.

proposals.name: Indispensable Allusion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a cultural, historical, or textual reference is necessary to the joke and creates a precise collision; score 0 when the reference is interchangeable or merely decorative.
proposals.rationale: R14, R43, and R54 make their references structurally important. R27 and R49 illustrate how a name can instead function mainly as trivia without a clear comic hinge.

proposals.name: Phonetic Reframing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a sound or spelling shift creates a natural alternate phrase with a vivid meaning; score 0 when resemblance alone supplies no coherent new phrase.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R41 turn familiar sounds into sharply different images. R03 and R39 show how simple name blending can receive credit even when the phonetic transformation is less fully developed.

proposals.name: Concrete Escalating Image
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when specific sensory or visual details escalate toward an unexpected, memorable image; score 0 when the entry remains abstract or stops before developing an image.
proposals.rationale: R47’s yellow champagne, R53’s rejected bills and mourners, and R55’s escalating mooning targets make their premises tangible. R36 and R48 remain largely undeveloped category labels.

proposals.name: Logical Load-Bearing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when each clause supports an intelligible paradox that withstands literal inspection before collapsing; score 0 when the contradiction is disconnected, obvious, or merely nonsensical.
proposals.rationale: R16, R45, and R60 build absurdity through recognizable reasoning. Their logic remains traceable, unlike entries whose oddity comes only from juxtaposition.

proposals.name: Familiar Phrase Repurposing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable slogan, formula, or stock expression is bent into a genuinely new meaning; score 0 when it is merely repeated or superficially altered.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R42 repurpose familiar slogan-like language, while R14 adapts a recognizable scriptural-sports formula. R25 and R31 show how discussing a familiar frame is weaker than transforming it.

proposals.name: Intentional Fragment Payoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when omission, incompletion, or a title fragment is clearly itself a deliberate comic device; score 0 when the text simply reads like an unfinished submission.
proposals.rationale: R40, R46, and R59 are fragments whose missing material may invite a purposeful comic completion. R34, R37, and R50 demonstrate how similar stubs can lack an evident internal payoff.

proposals.name: Meta-Awareness With Payload
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when awareness of the contest, genre, audience, or act of joking creates an additional mechanism; score 0 when the entry merely comments on itself without generating a joke.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R40 turn the contest or editorial frame into part of the comic device. R25 and R31 explicitly discuss the exercise, illustrating how meta-commentary can otherwise be mistaken for comic substance.

proposals.name: Construction Beyond Shock
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when crude, dark, or offensive material is transformed by exact wordplay, irony, or targeting; score 0 when shock or offensiveness is the only substantial mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R22, R26, and R39 invoke death, slurs, or danger, while R55 uses crude imagery. This criterion distinguishes mechanically precise transgression from material that relies mainly on provocation.

proposals.name: Identity-Specific Predicate
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the named person’s recognizable identity makes the chosen action, wording, or adverb unusually apt; score 0 when the person could be replaced without changing the joke.
proposals.rationale: R09, R21, R24, and R54 tie the named figures to drinking, circumspection, clothing, or mooring. R30 and R56 similarly depend on sports-specific identity and context.

proposals.name: Accessible With Second-Look Reward
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke parses immediately from the text yet rewards additional recognition or reflection; score 0 when it depends on obscure knowledge before any comic mechanism is visible.
proposals.rationale: R08, R41, and R43 are understandable without specialist research while offering extra recognition. R15, R27, and R49 require identifying relatively obscure names before their mechanisms can be assessed.

proposals.name: Non-Arbitrary Concept Bridge
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when disparate ideas are joined by one discoverable, exact relationship; score 0 when they are merely placed together for surreal or random effect.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R23 juxtapose disparate material with relatively weak connecting logic. R43 and R45 show stronger cases where the unusual elements are tied by one precise, intelligible relation.

proposals.name: Credit and locality metadata
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of visible bylines, contributor names, hometowns, or co-credit parentheticals. Do not judge whether these credits are good, prestigious, or relevant.
proposals.rationale: Visible credits appear in R02, R05, R29, and R41. They may proxy author familiarity or established participation rather than properties of the submitted joke itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's reputation, practice, or social standing

proposals.name: Celebrity-reference density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of recognizable public figures, institutions, brands, or famous cultural references. Do not judge whether the references are funny, apt, or well chosen.
proposals.rationale: R11, R18, R38, and R48 use conspicuous named figures or institutions. Familiarity with such names can influence processing independently of the entry's contest quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Submission-template residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of headings, labels, prompt restatements, answer markers, quote numbers, colons, or unfinished-looking scaffolding. Do not judge whether the formatting is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R22, R26, R42, R50, R56, and R60 retain labels such as “Quote,” “Answer,” or category scaffolding. These traces may reflect preparation or copy-editing processes rather than humor.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing or submission-process conventions

proposals.name: Orthographic and encoding anomalies
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of misspellings, malformed characters, unusual transliterations, missing accents, or visibly corrupted typography. Do not judge whether the anomalies help or hurt the entry.
proposals.rationale: R09 contains a malformed character, while R34 and R47 contain conspicuous spelling or transliteration irregularities. Such artifacts can predict textual handling without representing the underlying joke.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing, transcription, or data-ingestion pipeline

proposals.name: House-style quotation format
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of a polished quoted utterance followed by a speaker attribution and parenthetical contributor credit. Do not judge whether this presentation is elegant or effective.
proposals.rationale: R11, R20, R46, R48, R53, and R57 repeatedly use the same newspaper-style quotation-and-attribution mold. Format fluency may proxy practiced participation and can also accompany genuine writing skill.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice and familiarity with the contest format

proposals.name: Title-only compression
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry is a very short title, slogan, label, or noun phrase without explanation or elaboration. Do not judge whether the brevity is clever or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R02, R04, R10, R15, R25, R31, R51, and R55 are highly compressed one-liners. Extreme brevity may correlate with a submitter's strategy or familiarity, while concise writing can also genuinely affect quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission strategy and venue conventions

proposals.name: First-association literalness
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry makes a direct, literal, immediately obvious association with the prompt rather than an indirect or layered one. Do not judge whether the association is original or funny.
proposals.rationale: R02, R15, R31, and R51 offer compact, immediately legible oxymoron associations, while R19 and R60 use direct answer-question constructions. Early-stream or prompt-saturation effects could leave this textual fingerprint, though association choice can also bear on quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream and prompt saturation

proposals.name: Regional familiarity markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of Washington-area places, local teams, regional institutions, or geographically specific references. Do not judge whether the local references are appealing or relevant.
proposals.rationale: R07 and R14 name McLean and Takoma Park, while R06 invokes Detroit and the Pacers and R49 invokes Tysons Corner. Geographic familiarity may shape processing independently of the entry's construction.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience geography and local familiarity

proposals.name: Period-specific cultural residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of references to technologies, celebrities, institutions, or events strongly tied to a particular historical period. Do not judge whether the references are timely, dated, or amusing.
proposals.rationale: R09 invokes VCRs, R11 invokes Joey Buttafuoco, and R13 references the QE II and the Super Bowl. These temporal fingerprints may proxy when or for whom the text was produced rather than its intrinsic contest quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing and historical audience context

proposals.name: Taboo-content visibility
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of sexual, anatomical, bodily, death-related, violent, or otherwise taboo wording. Do not judge whether the material is tasteful, shocking, or funny.
proposals.rationale: R13 includes mooning and bodily imagery, R33 includes breasts, and R60 includes a codpiece; R28 also invokes a death camp. Taboo visibility can affect attention or social response independently of the entry's formal quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience norms and social-reception dynamics

proposals.name: Prompt-shaped comic payoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry exploits the contest prompt's specific mechanism so deeply that the joke depends on that format; score 0 when it could be transplanted unchanged into almost any prompt.
proposals.rationale: The format-specific turns in R38 and R46 feel purpose-built, while generic responses such as R11 and R45 appear more interchangeable.

proposals.name: Adverb–utterance lock
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the final adverb is grammatically natural, character-revealing, and creates a precise second meaning for the quoted utterance; score 0 when it is merely decorative or loosely attached.
proposals.rationale: R17, R26, R43, and R60 all derive their force from unusually exact matches between speaker, wording, and adverb.

proposals.name: Reference as comic machinery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a required famous person or institution actively generates the joke through a distinctive association; score 0 when the reference is only an attached name-drop.
proposals.rationale: The identities in R04 and R17 make the lines work, whereas a merely present celebrity or institution would satisfy the prompt without adding much.

proposals.name: Escalating micro-story
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when each successive line advances a compact situation toward a sharper, surprising payoff; score 0 when the lines merely repeat a rhyme or list disconnected details.
proposals.rationale: R03, R28, and R47 build recognizable situations that intensify before their final lines.

proposals.name: Form control under constraint
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when rhyme, meter, syntax, and required opening material all feel deliberate and fluent; score 0 when formal requirements are met only mechanically or disrupt natural language.
proposals.rationale: The limericks in R03, R28, and R47 show controlled form, while many short category responses provide little evidence of comparable craftsmanship.

proposals.name: High semantic compression
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every word contributes a distinct layer of premise, reference, or punchline and the entry remains immediately interpretable; score 0 when brevity produces genericness or incompleteness.
proposals.rationale: The compact shirt concepts in R06, R32, and R39 carry substantial comic implication in very few words.

proposals.name: Format-native visualizability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording would become an instantly legible, funny artifact in the requested medium, including layout or implied visual context; score 0 when it is only an abstract phrase with no medium-specific force.
proposals.rationale: R06, R32, and R39 are unusually usable as shirt backs, while a merely witty sentence would not exploit that format.

proposals.name: Stable false logic
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an apparently sensible statement survives an initial reading but collapses under a precise, internally coherent contradiction; score 0 when it is simply nonsensical or conventionally paradoxical.
proposals.rationale: R46, R48, R49, and R58 construct believable reasoning whose flaw becomes funnier on inspection.

proposals.name: Layered semantic collision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when two meanings or frames interact to create a second, stronger comic interpretation; score 0 when the apparent ambiguity has only one reading or is accidental.
proposals.rationale: R10, R14, and R38 each combine a familiar phrase or situation with an unexpected literal or contextual frame.

proposals.name: Exact two-reading wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the altered word or phrase supports two clear, related readings and the change is minimal but consequential; score 0 when it is merely a misspelling, loose homophone, or one-step pun.
proposals.rationale: The card-favored puns in R13, R15, and R24 suggest that simple word substitution can be over-credited, unlike the more structurally layered collision in R14.

proposals.name: Non-obvious specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry chooses a precise, unexpected target or detail that makes the joke uniquely identifiable; score 0 when it uses the first generic association available for the category.
proposals.rationale: R07, R21, and R30 rely on familiar stock constructions, whereas entries such as R40 and R59 derive more from sharply selected concepts.

proposals.name: Allusion accessibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the necessary cultural or factual reference is recognizable to a broad newspaper audience and still leaves room for transformation; score 0 when understanding depends on obscure knowledge unexplained by the text.
proposals.rationale: The obscure references in R18, R41, and R53 make comprehension costly, while the public figures used in R17 and R60 are more immediately usable.

proposals.name: Answer completeness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry supplies a finished, independently readable answer with a discernible comic point; score 0 when it merely repeats a category heading, gives a fragment, or stops before the joke begins.
proposals.rationale: R02, R22, R37, and R50 are headings or setups without completed examples, a weakness a text-sensitive judge can detect directly.

proposals.name: Targeted comic proportionality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comic target is clear and the intensity of the material is proportionate to the idea being explored; score 0 when shock, insult, or atrocity reference substitutes for an actual comic mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R12 and R25 use inflammatory references whose provocation overwhelms their wordplay, indicating a quality dimension beyond formal cleverness.

proposals.name: Surface polish
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when spelling, grammar, punctuation, and presentation are clean enough that attention stays on the joke; score 0 when avoidable errors or malformed setup materially obstruct reading.
proposals.rationale: The misspelling in R51, the malformed exchange in R54, and the awkward wording in R18 show how surface defects can undermine otherwise recognizable premises.

proposals.name: Prompt-scaffold residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry retains prompt labels, category stems, answer/question scaffolding, or visibly unfinished template language. Judge only presence of this feature; do not judge whether it is good or funny.
proposals.rationale: Such residue can trigger structural heuristics independently of entry quality. It appears in the category fragments of R06, R13, and R44, and in the answer framing of R35.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Fragmentary compression
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry is a bare fragment, title, heading, or extremely compressed one-line response rather than a syntactically developed passage. Do not judge whether the brevity is effective or ineffective.
proposals.rationale: Length and completeness are easy text-model proxies unrelated to intrinsic contest merit. Examples include the title-like R26, the unfinished-looking R21, and the short heading in R39.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Orthography and encoding noise
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of misspellings, unusual transliterations, encoding artifacts, conspicuous capitalization, or nonstandard punctuation. Rate only the amount of irregularity, never whether it improves or harms the entry.
proposals.rationale: Surface irregularities can attract disproportionate model attention without representing humor quality. The slice includes the encoding artifact in R02, the spelling error in R34, and the unusual name spelling in R20.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Proper-noun load
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry relies on named people, places, organizations, brands, institutions, or other specific entities. Do not judge whether the references are apt, recognizable, or amusing.
proposals.rationale: Named-entity density can act as a topical or familiarity proxy rather than a quality measure. It is prominent in R11, R18, R35, and R50.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Period-specific anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry contains references strongly tied to a particular historical period, technology, celebrity cycle, or cultural moment. Judge only temporal anchoring, not whether it is timely or funny.
proposals.rationale: Production timing can leave dated references in the text, which may affect reader familiarity independently of merit; the same timing can also shape genuine topical fit. Examples are the VCR reference in R03, the QE II and Super Bowl references in R16, and Reagan in R38.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing / historical moment

proposals.name: Local-community anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry contains Washington-area locality signals, local institutions, or geographically specific community references. Do not judge whether the locality makes the entry better.
proposals.rationale: Local familiarity can influence how text is processed while remaining external to the entry's intrinsic quality. Washington-area signals appear in R02, R09, R51, and R59.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience/following and local-community familiarity

proposals.name: Genre-template fluency
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry follows a highly recognizable contest subgenre template, such as quoted speech followed by a named speaker and an adverbial tag. Rate conformity only; do not judge whether the resulting joke is good.
proposals.rationale: Experienced entrants may leave a polished, conventional template fingerprint that models can reward; practice may also genuinely improve writing, so this is mixed. The repeated construction is visible in R11, R18, R42, R52, and R57.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Collaborative-credit signature
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text visibly signals shared authorship or coordinated submission through multiple names, semicolon-separated credits, or phrases such as “also.” Do not judge whether collaboration helped the entry.
proposals.rationale: Joint production can create a recognizable textual-credit pattern that affects interpretation, while collaboration may also genuinely improve an entry. Clear examples are R22, R24, R49, and R60.
proposals.upstream_parent: social collaboration / shared authorship

proposals.name: Documentary framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry is presented as a quotation, report, excerpt, transcription, source attribution, or numbered continuation rather than as direct authored text. Judge only the framing, not its authenticity or quality.
proposals.rationale: Source-like packaging can lend authority or salience to text without changing its intrinsic humor. The framing appears in “From a sign” in R08, “Quote 7” in R19, and the letter setup in R39.
proposals.upstream_parent: source provenance / editorial assistance

proposals.name: Late-riff residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry shows a second-order, self-referential, defensive, or residual riff that reads as reacting to already-obvious approaches. Judge only the textual signs; do not infer actual submission order or judge originality.
proposals.rationale: A crowded stream or late arrival could leave this fingerprint, and the resulting reaction can sometimes affect genuine quality, so it is mixed. Self-aware or meta-presentational traces occur in R14, R41, and R46.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / submission timing
